front.label: Front matter
front.intro: How to read this book, and the rules it keeps.

chapters.title: The cover
chapters.blurb: A Cape Dutch family that kept marrying British women, changed one letter of its name in a war, and came off the train at Johannesburg with nothing.

chapters.title: About
chapters.blurb: Every claim carries one of five words and every correction is published; a living person is named with relationships and town and country, and nothing more.

chapters.title: Method
chapters.blurb: Every claim carries a label saying how well it is known.

parts.title: One letter, and the Karoo it came from
parts.intro: The home page opens on one letter of a surname, changed on purpose. This part starts with the name itself, with the forenames that outlast a surname, and with the Atlas: a band of Karoo and north-eastern Cape districts, Graaff-Reinet and Cradock among them, a jump of four hundred miles to the Rand, and one district that shares the surname and is not the family at all.

chapters.title: The Name
chapters.blurb: Booyzen is one family's deliberate break from a mass surname, and the distribution figures say so.

chapters.title: The forenames
chapters.blurb: A forename is inherited property: it travels through daughters and outlives a change of surname.

chapters.title: The Atlas
chapters.blurb: Where this family was, plotted from latitude and longitude: Karoo and north-eastern Cape districts, and the Rand.

parts.title: The line, and the names around it
parts.intro: The descent from the Spine, drawn three ways, and then every family name the archive has researched. Each family page is counted from the archive's own people, households and register. The Mountjoys are where the line meets the Booyzens; the Barrys gave the family its English forenames, and the Kolbes were a German tailor's family.

chapters.title: The Spine
chapters.blurb: The descent from the grandmother back to a man with no dates and no parents; two links in it are in dispute.

parts.title: A war, a train and the Rand
parts.intro: One paragraph of family testimony names a war, a betrayal, an execution, a camp, a burned farm and a train, and the archive tests each claim in turn. Then the other end of the journey: a family that arrived from the Cape, settled in the southern and western suburbs of Johannesburg, and buried most of itself there.

chapters.title: The rebels
chapters.blurb: One paragraph of family testimony, with each of its claims taken apart and tested.

chapters.title: Johannesburg
chapters.blurb: What the record shows at the other end of the train: the southern and western suburbs, and the family buried there.

parts.title: Who married whom
parts.intro: A marriage is where two lines join, and it is also where a family chooses a town, a church and a witness. Every marriage a document places, the households assembled from them, the one marriage that folds the tree back on itself, the women through whom the forenames, the politics, the religion, the 1820 Settler descent and the German origins arrived, and a chart of blood relatives built around any person.

Each person page also belongs to The People and links back to it; each name page to Every Name; each place page to Places.
